name: Dark grapes
summary: Dark skins hold purple pigments (anthocyanins) and resveratrol that green grapes have little of. People who ate more grapes and raisins got type 2 diabetes less often, but no study has yet shown that dark grapes do more for health than green ones.
inIt: Grape polyphenols sit almost entirely in the skin. In a 2002 study of seven table grape varieties (four red, three white), the flesh was almost free of them.

Anthocyanins, the red, purple and black pigments, are what set dark grapes apart. Red varieties can make them and white (green) varieties cannot. In the four red table grapes studied in 2002, anthocyanins were the main polyphenols, 6.9 to 15.1 mg per 100 g of fresh grapes.

Green grapes have polyphenols too, of other kinds. In the three white varieties, flavan-3-ols (catechins and procyanidins) were the main ones, 5.2 to 8.1 mg per 100 g. Quercetin compounds are found in both red and white grapes; myricetin compounds only in red ones.

Darker doesn't always mean more polyphenols in total. In 2002, total polyphenols ranged from 11.5 mg per 100 g (Dominga, a white grape) to 36.1 mg (Flame Seedless, a red one). But a 2026 study found more total polyphenols and flavonoids in Shine Muscat, a green grape, than in the red Crimson Seedless and Red Globe.

Resveratrol is in grape skins in small amounts, mostly bound to a sugar (piceid). In 36 grape juices, red juices held on average 4.7 mg of resveratrol in all its forms per litre and white juices 0.5 mg. A 150 ml glass of red juice would hold about 0.7 mg (calculated from those averages). In a meta-analysis of resveratrol supplement trials, blood pressure fell only in trials that used 300 mg a day or more, several hundred times as much; resveratrol pills are a different thing from grapes.

Concord grape juice, made from a dark American grape, is rich in these compounds: one 355 ml daily serving in a trial held 777 mg of polyphenols, 167 mg of them anthocyanins. In another trial, purple grape juice held 138 mg of anthocyanins per litre and white grape juice 1 mg.

The UK food table (CoFID) measures the basic nutrients. Per 100 g: red grapes 67 kcal, 17 g sugars, 1.3 g fibre and 213 mg potassium; raisins 256 kcal, 62.6 g sugars, 2.7 g fibre and 889 mg potassium; unsweetened grape juice 62 kcal, 16 g sugars and no fibre. It measures none of the anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols, quercetin or resveratrol, and a food has thousands of compounds no table tracks.

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, about AD 77)
lore.belief: Pliny wrote that freshly picked grapes cause wind and upset the stomach and bowels, so they were kept from people with fevers, especially in large amounts, and that they can bring on a heavy head and lethargy. Grapes left hanging in the air for a while, he said, were much less harmful, even good for the stomach, and refreshing for the sick, easing nausea and queasiness.
lore.note: No study on this page looked at wind, stomach upsets, nausea or drowsiness after eating grapes, or at people with a fever.

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, about AD 77)
lore.belief: Medical writers, Pliny reported, held that grapes kept in rain water were the most wholesome of all, though not pleasant to eat, and good for burning pains in the stomach, for bile from a disordered liver, for vomiting of bile and for cholera, for dropsy (swelling from fluid) and for burning fevers.
lore.note: No study has tested grapes, stored this way or any other, for stomach pain, liver trouble, cholera, fluid swelling or fever.

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, about AD 77)
lore.belief: Pliny wrote that raisins with their stones taken out were thought good for the bladder and for coughs (white raisins best for coughs), and for the windpipe and the kidneys, and that raisins eaten with pepper were used to cleanse the mouth and 'clear the brain'.
lore.note: No study on this page has tested raisins for coughs, the bladder or the kidneys. The few small trials of grape juice and grape powder on memory and attention ask a different question, and their results were mixed.

lore.who: Chinese medicine (the Mingyi Bielu and later physicians, quoted by Li Shizhen in 1578)
lore.belief: Chinese physicians wrote that grapes drive out excess water and help people pass urine (Mingyi Bielu), clear water from the bowels and treat painful, difficult urination (Zhen Quan), and that when the spots of smallpox would not come out, eating grapes, or drinking them ground in wine, worked very well (Su Song). Meng Shen warned that eating too many brings on a sudden, stifling restlessness and dims the eyes.
lore.note: No study on this page has tested grapes for passing urine, for pain when passing urine, or for smallpox, and none looked for restlessness or dim sight after eating many.

lore.who: China (Cao Pi, Emperor Wen of Wei, 3rd century AD, quoted by Su Song and Li Shizhen)
lore.belief: The emperor wrote to his ministers that grapes at the end of summer, eaten still wet with dew after a night of heavy drinking, were sweet but not cloying, cool but not cold, and took away restlessness and thirst; wine made from them, he said, made people drunk easily and let them sober up easily too.
lore.note: No study on this page has tested grapes for hangovers or thirst.

lore.belief: Genesis says Noah, a man of the soil, was the first to plant a vineyard; he drank its wine, became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. In the Talmud Rabbi Meir argued that the forbidden tree of Eden was a vine, because 'nothing brings wailing and trouble upon man even today other than wine'.

lore.belief: The spies Moses sent into Canaan cut a single cluster of grapes so heavy that two of them had to carry it on a frame, and brought it back with pomegranates and figs to show what the land produced. The prophets pictured peace as every family sitting under its own vine and fig tree, with no one to disturb them.

lore.who: Ancient Greece (Euripides, Bacchae, first staged 405 BC)
lore.belief: The Greeks honoured Dionysus, son of Semele, as the god who discovered 'the liquid drink of the grape' and brought it to mortals. In Euripides' play the prophet Teiresias says it frees wretched people from grief, gives them sleep and a way to forget their daily troubles, and that there is no other cure for hardships.
lore.note: This is about wine, not the fruit.

lore.belief: Jesus called himself 'the true vine', his Father the vine-grower and his followers the branches, which bear fruit only while they stay joined to the vine. At the Last Supper he gave his disciples the cup as his blood, and said he would not drink 'this fruit of the vine' again until he drank it new with them in his Father's kingdom.

lore.belief: The Qur'an counts grapevines among God's gifts, with palms, olives and pomegranates, and promises the righteous 'gardens and grapevines' in Paradise, where there are also rivers of wine 'delicious to those who drink'. On earth, it says, people take from palms and grapes both 'intoxicant and good provision', and another verse calls intoxicants a defilement from the work of Satan, to be avoided.

lore.who: Han China (Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, about 100 BC)
lore.belief: Sima Qian recorded that in Dayuan (the Ferghana valley in Central Asia) people made wine from grapes, and rich families stored more than ten thousand measures of it, some for decades without it spoiling. Han envoys brought the seeds home, the emperor had grapes and alfalfa planted on fertile land, and in time they grew beside his palaces as far as the eye could see.
lore.note: Li Shizhen's herbal of 1578 credits Zhang Qian, the first Han envoy to the west, with bringing grapes to China; the older history speaks only of Han envoys.

lore.who: Chinese medicine (Shennong's Classic of Materia Medica, quoted by Li Shizhen in 1578)
lore.belief: The Shennong classic says grapes treat aching, damp-stiff sinews and bones, boost energy, 'double strength' and strengthen the will, make people plump and hardy, help them bear hunger, wind and cold, and that eaten for a long time they 'lighten the body, keep away old age and lengthen the years'.
lore.note: No study has measured whether grapes slow ageing or lengthen life. In the evidence on this page, people in large US cohorts who ate more grapes and raisins got type 2 diabetes less often, which is a different question.

history.who: Ayurveda, traditional medicine of the Indian subcontinent
history.use: Fermented grapes, as a tonic called Drakshasava, for tiredness, weakness and heart disease.
history.note: No trial of Drakshasava for weakness or heart disease turned up in the searches for this page. It is a fermented preparation, not fresh grapes, and the grape trials on this page measured blood pressure, blood fats and blood vessel function, not heart disease itself.

history.who: Johanna Brandt's "grape cure" (South Africa and the US, book published 1928)
history.use: A diet of grapes promoted as a cure for cancer.
history.note: No trial has tested a grape diet against cancer, and none of the studies on this page measured cancer. The American Cancer Society listed the "grape cure" among unproven methods of cancer treatment in 1965 and again in 1974: there is no evidence that it works.

history.use: The idea that red wine explains why France had little heart disease despite a high-fat diet; grapes were later promoted on the back of it.
history.note: The French paradox was about wine and alcohol, a different exposure from grapes: wine adds alcohol, and the 1992 paper that named it pointed to alcohol damping down blood platelets. No study has tested whether eating grapes explains it; trials of grapes, grape juice and grape powder found only small, uncertain changes in blood pressure and blood fats, and none measured heart attacks.

tableFoods.label: A small bunch of red grapes (about 80 g)
A small box of raisins (about 30 g)
A small glass of grape juice (about 150 ml)

processing: Skin matters most: the polyphenols, including the anthocyanins that make dark grapes dark, are in the skin, not the flesh. Seeds and stems hold polyphenols too, and juice has less of them than the whole fruit. Grape seed extract is a different intervention from eating grapes.

Raisins are usually not dark grapes. The most common raisins, dark raisins, are usually made from Thompson Seedless, a green grape, so their dark colour doesn't come from dark grapes. Golden raisins are made from white Muscat grapes. Raisins are dried and concentrated: per 100 g the food table lists 62.6 g of sugars and 889 mg of potassium, against 17 g and 213 mg for fresh red grapes.

Juice has no fibre and more sugar per glass than a bunch of grapes has: the food table gives about 24 g of sugars in 150 ml of unsweetened grape juice and about 14 g in 80 g of red grapes (calculated from its values per 100 g). The table doesn't say which grapes its juice was made from. Many trials used 100% Concord grape juice, a dark juice; white grape juice has far fewer anthocyanins and about a tenth of the resveratrol.

Many trials used a freeze-dried powder made from fresh red, green and black grapes, seeded and seedless, ground and freeze-dried. It is made under the auspices of the California Table Grape Commission, which also funded some of the research. Because it is a mix of colours, trials of the powder can't say whether dark grapes do more than green ones.

Grape seed extract, resveratrol supplements and red wine are different exposures from grapes and are not covered by this page's findings. Wine adds alcohol; extracts and pills concentrate a few compounds in amounts no one gets from fruit.
whatStudiesDid: Trials of Concord grape juice gave about 6 to 9 ml per kg of body weight a day (for a 70 kg adult about 420 to 630 ml), or a fixed 355 ml a day, for 2 weeks to 4 months, against a drink matched for sugar and calories but without polyphenols. Trials of freeze-dried grape powder (a mix of red, green and black grapes) gave it for 2 weeks to 6 months; in one, two 36 g packets a day (72 g, said to equal 3 servings of fresh grapes) for 6 months. Raisin trials gave raisins as snacks three times a day for 12 weeks and compared them with processed snacks. One small trial compared a single glass of purple grape juice with sugar-matched white grape juice. The cohort studies asked people how often they ate grapes or raisins, without recording the colour.

findings.population: Grapes and raisins in general (colour not recorded): US nurses and male health professionals, 187,382 people followed for up to about 24 years
whyThisGrade: Observational: people who eat more grapes may differ in other ways, even after adjustment
Diet was reported on questionnaires
One analysis of three cohorts; the participants were mostly white health professionals in the US
Grapes and raisins were asked about together, and their colour was not recorded, so it says nothing about dark grapes in particular
findings.summary: In three US cohorts (66,105 women in the Nurses' Health Study, 85,104 in the Nurses' Health Study II and 36,173 men in the Health Professionals Follow-up Study), 12,198 people developed type 2 diabetes. With each fruit adjusted for the others and for personal, lifestyle and diet factors, every 3 extra servings a week of grapes or raisins went with a hazard ratio of 0.88 (95% confidence interval 0.83 to 0.93). The same increase in fruit juice (apple, orange, grapefruit and other juices) went with a higher risk, 1.08 (1.05 to 1.11). In the full text, swapping 3 servings a week of fruit juice for grapes or raisins went with a 19% lower risk (14% to 24% lower). The study was funded by the US National Institutes of Health. It recorded grapes and raisins together, not their colour.
findings.bottomLine: In three large US cohorts, people who ate more grapes and raisins were less likely to develop type 2 diabetes (12% lower risk per 3 servings a week), while fruit juice went with higher risk. This is a link from questionnaires, not proof, and grape colour wasn't recorded.
findings.label: Type 2 diabetes
findings.line: 12% lower risk per 3 servings a week in US cohorts (a link, not proof)

studies.title: Fruit consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes: results from three prospective longitudinal cohort studies.

findings.population: Adults in randomised trials of grape products: freeze-dried whole grape powder (a mix of red, green and black grapes), raisins (usually from green grapes) and Concord grape juice
whyThisGrade: The 2023 meta-analysis rated the certainty of the fall in systolic pressure as low (GRADE)
Results varied between trials (I² 64%), and juice, the darkest product tested, showed no clear effect
Most trials were small and short; the raisin trials compared raisins with processed snacks, not with no snack
The powder is made under the auspices of the California Table Grape Commission; the Concord juice blood pressure trial was funded by US National Institutes of Health grants
findings.summary: A 2023 meta-analysis of 30 randomised trials of grape products found systolic blood pressure 3.17 mmHg lower (95% confidence interval 0.99 to 5.36 lower), rated low certainty, and no clear change in diastolic pressure. Whole grape products (raisins and grape powder) went with 2.69 mmHg lower systolic pressure (0.57 to 4.81 lower); grape juice did not change it clearly. In a crossover trial of 64 adults with high-normal or mildly high blood pressure, 100% Concord grape juice (7 ml per kg a day for 8 weeks) did not change 24-hour blood pressure compared with a matched placebo drink. In a 30-day crossover trial in 24 men with metabolic syndrome, freeze-dried grape powder lowered systolic pressure compared with placebo. In a 12-week trial in 46 adults, systolic pressure fell by 6.0 to 10.2 mmHg with raisin snacks and didn't change with processed snacks; in a 12-week trial in 51 people with type 2 diabetes it was 8.7 mmHg lower with raisins than with processed snacks. No trial compared dark with green grapes.
findings.bottomLine: In a meta-analysis of 30 small trials of grape products, systolic blood pressure was about 3 mmHg lower, with low certainty. Raisins and grape powder (a mix of grape colours) went with a fall; grape juice, including dark Concord juice, did not clearly change blood pressure.
findings.label: Blood pressure
findings.line: Lower with raisins and grape powder, not clearly with juice (small trials)

findings.outcome: Blood fats (LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, triglycerides)
findings.population: Adults in randomised trials of grape products: freeze-dried grape powder or pomace (the skins and seeds left after pressing), grape juice, and grape seed or skin extracts
whyThisGrade: Meta-analyses pool grape powder, pomace, juice and extracts; extracts are a different intervention
In the grape juice trials there was no change in LDL
Small trials (8 to 50 people each in the 2020 meta-analysis) and some had no dummy placebo
Results varied between trials (I² 74.7% for HDL); certainty wasn't rated in the abstracts
findings.summary: A 2020 meta-analysis of 24 randomised trials (1,205 people; full text read) found LDL cholesterol 6.3 mg/dL lower (95% confidence interval 3.0 to 9.5 lower), total cholesterol 7.6 mg/dL lower, triglycerides 14.5 mg/dL lower and HDL 1.4 mg/dL higher with grape products of any kind compared with placebo. Of the trials, 11 tested grape powder or pomace, 5 grape juice and 8 extracts. By type of product, LDL was 6.3 mg/dL lower with whole grape products (grape powder or pomace; 1.6 to 11.0 lower), not clearly changed with grape seed extracts (4.3 lower, 10.9 lower to 2.2 higher) and unchanged with grape juice (0.21 mg/dL higher, 7.6 lower to 8.1 higher). A 2019 meta-analysis of 48 trials of grape products in any form found LDL 5.0 mg/dL lower, total cholesterol 6.2 lower and triglycerides 7.6 lower, with no change in HDL. Neither looked at grape colour.
findings.bottomLine: Meta-analyses of grape products found LDL cholesterol about 5 to 6 mg/dL lower, a small change. The fall came from grape powder and pomace; in grape juice trials LDL didn't change, and the pooled results mix in extracts, so the effect of eating grapes is uncertain.
findings.label: LDL cholesterol and blood fats
findings.line: LDL a little lower with grape powder, unchanged with juice; uncertain

findings.population: Purple (Concord) grape juice in small studies of people with coronary artery disease and healthy smokers; freeze-dried grape powder (a mix of red, green and black grapes) in men with metabolic syndrome
whyThisGrade: When trials were pooled in a 2023 meta-analysis, there was no clear effect on endothelial function
The single studies were very small (15 to 26 people) and lasted 2 to 4 weeks; the first had no comparison group
Flow-mediated dilation is a measure of the blood vessel lining, not a heart attack or stroke
Who funded these vascular studies isn't stated in the abstracts read; in Concord juice research elsewhere (the memory trials), the juice maker supplied the juice
findings.summary: In a 1999 study without a comparison group, 15 adults with coronary artery disease drank purple grape juice (about 7.7 ml per kg a day) for 14 days; flow-mediated dilation, how much the arm artery widens, rose from 2.2% to 6.4%, and LDL resisted oxidation longer. In a double-blind crossover trial in 26 healthy smokers, 2 weeks of Concord grape juice improved flow-mediated dilation and artery stiffness compared with placebo, and blunted the worsening right after smoking a cigarette. In 24 men with metabolic syndrome, 30 days of freeze-dried grape powder raised flow-mediated dilation compared with placebo. But a 2023 meta-analysis of 30 trials of grape products found no clear effect on endothelial function overall. No trial measured heart attacks or strokes.
findings.bottomLine: Very small, short studies of purple Concord grape juice and of grape powder found that arteries widened better, but when trials were pooled there was no clear effect on blood vessel function. No study measured heart attacks or strokes.
findings.label: Blood vessel function
findings.line: Better in very small studies, no clear effect when trials were pooled

findings.population: Concord grape juice in older adults with mild memory decline and in healthy middle-aged mothers; purple vs white grape juice in young adults; freeze-dried grape powder (red, green and blue-black grapes) in older adults with mild memory decline
whyThisGrade: Five small trials of grapes themselves, with 10 to 25 people each
Many different tests: some improved, many didn't, and no meta-analysis was possible
A 2022 systematic review rated most trials' risk of bias as unclear
The Concord juice was provided by Welch Foods, and one trial had a Welch's employee as an author
findings.summary: A 2022 systematic review found 8 randomised trials of grapes and cognition (474 people); 3 of them tested extracts, which are a different intervention. Of the trials of grapes themselves: in 12 older adults with memory decline, 12 weeks of Concord grape juice improved verbal learning but not recall; in 21 such adults, 16 weeks of juice reduced memory interference and changed brain activation on scans; in 25 working mothers, 355 ml of Concord juice a day for 12 weeks improved immediate spatial memory and driving performance in a simulator compared with placebo; and in 10 older adults with mild memory decline, 6 months of grape powder kept brain metabolism stable on PET scans while it fell with placebo, with no difference in test scores. One trial compared dark with green directly: in 20 young adults, a glass of purple grape juice improved reaction time on an attention task and calmness 20 minutes later compared with sugar-matched white grape juice, with no effect on memory. The review authors said differences in design, amounts and tests made the trials hard to compare.
findings.bottomLine: A few very small trials of Concord grape juice and grape powder found better scores on some memory or attention tests and no change on others. One trial found purple juice beat white juice on attention 20 minutes later. The evidence is too thin to know whether grapes help thinking.
findings.label: Memory and thinking
findings.line: Better on some tests, not others, in a few very small trials

findings.outcome: Blood sugar: after meals, fasting and HbA1c
findings.population: Raisins (usually made from green grapes) in healthy adults, people with prediabetes and people with type 2 diabetes; grape products of various kinds in a meta-analysis
whyThisGrade: The raisin trials were small (46 and 51 people) and compared raisins with processed snacks, so they show raisins vs those snacks, not raisins vs nothing
Glycaemic index studies measure one meal, not long-term health
In the meta-analysis of grape products, fasting glucose was slightly higher, not lower, and HbA1c didn't change
Who funded the raisin trials isn't stated in the abstracts read
findings.summary: Glycaemic index studies found raisins raise blood sugar less than glucose: a glycaemic index of about 49 to 62 in healthy, trained and prediabetic adults, and an estimated 66 for Corinthian raisins in healthy people and people with type 2 diabetes. In a 12-week trial in 46 adults, with raisins three times a day blood sugar after meals fell by 13.1 mg/dL and HbA1c by 0.12 percentage points, both more than with processed snacks; fasting glucose didn't change. In a 12-week trial in 51 people with type 2 diabetes, blood sugar after meals was 23% lower with raisins than with processed snacks, while the falls in fasting glucose and HbA1c could be chance. A 2021 meta-analysis of 29 trials of grapes and grape products (1,297 people) found no change in HbA1c or fasting insulin, slightly higher fasting glucose (1.19 mg/dL) and lower insulin resistance (HOMA-IR 0.54 lower).
findings.bottomLine: Raisins raise blood sugar less than glucose, and in two small trials raisin snacks went with lower blood sugar after meals than processed snacks did. Across 29 trials of grape products, long-term blood sugar (HbA1c) didn't change. Raisins are usually made from green grapes.
findings.label: Blood sugar
findings.line: Lower after meals with raisin snacks in two small trials; HbA1c unchanged

A newer study found a green grape (Shine Muscat) with more total polyphenols than two red ones, so colour is only part of the story. More of a compound in the fruit doesn't show a health effect.

whoShouldBeCareful.note: Whole grapes are the right size and shape to block a small child's airway. Doctors have described children who choked on whole grapes, some fatally, and called for wider awareness that grapes and similar round foods are a choking hazard for young children.

The UK food table lists 16 g of sugars per 100 g of unsweetened grape juice (about 24 g in a 150 ml glass), 62.6 g per 100 g of raisins (about 19 g in a 30 g box) and 17 g per 100 g of red grapes (about 14 g in an 80 g bunch). Juice has no fibre. A 355 ml serving of Concord grape juice in one trial held 54 g of sugars. If you are managing blood sugar, talk to your doctor or dietitian about juice and dried fruit.

The UK food table lists 889 mg of potassium per 100 g of raisins (about 267 mg in a 30 g box), against 213 mg per 100 g of red grapes and 55 mg per 100 g of grape juice. If you have been told to limit potassium, talk to your doctor or renal dietitian about raisins and other dried fruit.

cautions: Grapes and raisins can poison dogs: in a Swiss series, all 15 dogs with grape or raisin poisoning had severe kidney injury and 8 survived.
Grapes and grape juice are not a treatment for high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes or memory problems. Anything clearly out of range in your results is worth discussing with your doctor.
Fruit juice in general went with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes in the large US cohorts, and juice has none of the fruit's fibre.
unknowns: No study of people has compared dark with green grapes on health outcomes or lifespan. Dark grapes hold anthocyanins that green grapes lack, and red juice has more resveratrol, but whether that changes anything in the body over years is not known. The only head-to-head trial found that a single glass of purple juice beat white juice on an attention test 20 minutes later, in 20 people.

No study of people has measured grapes and death from any cause, or lifespan. A study in mice found that a high-fat diet with 5% grape powder (a mix of red, green and black grapes) went with longer survival than the same diet without it (hazard ratio 0.715, 100 mice per group); mice are not people.
The cohort link with less type 2 diabetes is for grapes and raisins together, colour not recorded, and can't show cause.

Most trials used Concord juice, a freeze-dried powder that mixes grape colours, or raisins usually made from green grapes; very few tested fresh dark grapes as people eat them. Many were small, short and supplied or funded by Welch's or the California Table Grape Commission.

Resveratrol supplements and red wine are different exposures. Supplement trials use hundreds of milligrams a day, far more than grapes hold, and in an Italian cohort of 783 older adults, the amount of resveratrol from diet (measured in urine) did not go with how many died over 9 years (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% confidence interval 0.54 to 1.17, for the lowest vs highest quarter). Wine adds alcohol.
It isn't known which compounds explain any effect. The food table measures sugars, fibre and minerals but none of the polyphenols, and a food has thousands of compounds no table tracks.
